name: Yusuf Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm not much of a talker, so you might have to dig. Kenji, my brother, is the one who likes meetings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My brother and I own Lower Fold Farm, 160 hectares that our dad bought in the eighties. I do the hands side: about 200 beef cattle we finish for the abattoir, plus potatoes and some barley. I'm up at six, feed round with the old Ford tractor, then it's the potato store or the fields depending on the month. Kenji does the books and the buyers, which suits me, because I can't stand a phone ringing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Claire's a dental nurse in town, and we've got Ellie, fourteen, and Sam, eleven. We built a house on the edge of the farm with a mortgage, about half paid now. Money's fine, we've a good bit saved and the land behind us, so I don't lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. At the auction mart I'd say the same thing I say about most new kit: wait and see what it does in a wet year. I don't go online much, Claire does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and I'm happy with that. Kenji might use something for the paperwork, but the cattle don't care. My tractor is older than my daughter Ellie, and it still starts every morning without a software update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Same cattle, same potato contract, same feed merchant. We'd keep paying the house down and leave the savings alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like a world where the next ten years look like the last ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything already on your mind about the farm, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beef prices go up and down, and the potato buyer squeezes us every spring. But we've done this for twenty years. As long as Kenji and I keep talking, the farm's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kenji might use something for the paperwork. Would you ever?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't see why I'd start. If I need a form filled, Kenji fills it, and if Kenji's away, it waits.

say: I'd tell the auction mart to **wait and see** how new kit does in a wet year.
I'd leave **online talk** to Claire, because I rarely go online.
think: **Nothing changes** for me, and I'm happy with that.
Kenji might use it for **paperwork**, but the cattle don't care.
do: Keep the **same cattle**, potato contract and feed merchant.
Keep paying the **house mortgage** down and leave savings alone.
feel: **Calm**, because the next ten years look like the last ten.
S0.quote: My tractor is older than my daughter Ellie, and it still starts every morning without a software update.
fieldNote: Yusuf is a **landowner** with a brother who handles the office side.
His usual worries, **prices and buyers**, are old ones he's used to.
He has **never used AI** and sees no reason to.

steps.text: Keep the same beef cattle, potato contract and feed merchant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices and not much use in a muddy field. If people asked, I'd say farming changes slowly and that's no bad thing. At the mart we'd talk about it for five minutes and then go back to cattle prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it changes Kenji's side, not mine. The potato buyer would probably send contracts through some AI system and want answers in an hour. That's annoying, but it's Kenji's annoyance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do much. Kenji can take a course if he wants. I'd wait and see what the neighbours do with any robots before we spend a penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little irritated that everyone keeps telling me the world's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would feel this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire, maybe. The dental practice books appointments and sends reminders, and that's the sort of thing a program does. My wife Claire is the one with the computer job in our house, and I never thought I'd say that about a dental nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a neighbour bought a robot that worked, would you follow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not quickly. I'd want to see it run three or four seasons, break down and get fixed. By then the price has dropped and the bugs are out.

say: I'd say AI is fine for **offices**, not much use in a muddy field.
I'd say farming **changes slowly**, and that's no bad thing.
think: It changes **Kenji's side** of the farm, not mine.
The potato buyer would want **answers in an hour**, which is Kenji's problem.
do: Leave any **AI course** to Kenji if he wants one.
Watch the **neighbours' robots** for several seasons before spending anything.
feel: Calm, a little **irritated** at being told the world's changing.
S1.quote: My wife Claire is the one with the computer job in our house, and I never thought I'd say that about a dental nurse.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption landing on the **office side** of his life, and even on Claire's job.
His rule is to wait **three or four seasons** before following anyone.
Ownership of land and a brother on the paperwork give him **a buffer**.

steps.text: Keep doing the cattle and potato work by hand
Watch neighbours' robots for three or four seasons before buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody had better slow this down. At the mart I'd say the big farms will buy robots and the rest of us will be squeezed. I'd vote for whoever promised to look after family farms, whatever colour they were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm not worried about losing the farm, it's ours. I'm worried about being the slow one. If the big potato growers have robots working nights by 2031, the buyer pays their price, and our potatoes don't pay anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop the plan for a new potato store, that's eighty thousand we'd keep in the bank. I'd talk to Kenji about renting the potato ground to Hendersons next door, who'd buy robots straight away. I'd keep the cattle, because that's what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not frightened, we've got the land. But it's the first time I'd feel the farm getting away from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots around 2031. What happens on Lower Fold in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenji's half changes in 2028: buyers, contracts, the bank all using AI. Mine changes in 2031. Three years is how long I'd have to decide whether Lower Fold Farm is still a farm or just land we rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the cattle. Even if a robot could do it better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even then, for a while. I don't know what I'd do with myself otherwise. But Kenji would ask if we can afford my stubbornness, and he'd have a point.

say: I'd say somebody should **slow this down** before big farms squeeze us.
I'd vote for whoever **backs family farms**, whatever their colour.
think: The farm is ours, but I'd be **the slow one**.
Robot-run growers could make our **potatoes not pay** by 2031.
do: Cancel the **£80,000 potato store** and keep the money in the bank.
Talk to Kenji about **renting the potato ground** to Hendersons next door.
Keep the **cattle**, because that's what I know.
feel: Worried, feeling the **farm slip away** for the first time.
S2.quote: Three years is how long I'd have to decide whether Lower Fold Farm is still a farm or just land we rent out.
fieldNote: Owning land protects him, but **falling behind** threatens the income.
He'd let a neighbour automate rather than **learn it himself**.
He's honest that keeping cattle is partly **stubbornness**.

steps.text: Cancel the £80,000 potato store and keep the cash
Rent the potato ground to Hendersons next door
Vote for whoever promises to protect family farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've a few years to see it coming, so let's watch closely. At the mart I'd be asking who's tried what. I'd tell Ellie and Sam to take school seriously, which I'd say anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could manage this one. Five years to the AI and eight to the robots is long enough for others to find the problems. If the robots work, we rent the potato land out and I keep the cattle going a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do almost nothing in the first year, honestly, except keep saving. Around 2030 Kenji and I would sit down and agree a line: if the potato price drops below a set figure, we rent the land out. I'd keep the cattle till I'm sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's more like watching a storm on the hills than standing in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on. What does it mean that the robots come three years after the thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my side lasts longest, which I'm glad of. But by 2031 the buyers' computers will know my costs better than I do. I'd be doing the same jobs with someone smarter than me setting the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do almost nothing in the first year. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But in my experience the farmer who buys first pays twice. I've watched three neighbours go broke buying the newest machine, and none of them went broke waiting.

say: I'd say we've **a few years** to watch closely.
I'd ask around the mart about **who's tried what**.
think: I could **manage this one**, because others will find the problems first.
If robots work, we **rent the potato land** and I keep the cattle longer.
do: **Keep saving** and do little else in the first year.
Agree a **price line** with Kenji around 2030 for renting out the potato land.
feel: Uneasy, like watching a **storm on the hills**.
S3.quote: I've watched three neighbours go broke buying the newest machine, and none of them went broke waiting.
fieldNote: Five years suits his **wait-and-see** style: others pay for the mistakes.
He senses a loss of **bargaining power** to AI-driven buyers.
His caution rests on a story about **neighbours going broke** on new machines.

steps.text: Keep saving and hold off on new machinery
Set a potato price line with Kenji for renting out the land

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in farming, that's ten harvests. People would have time to sort it, and so would the government. I'd not get worked up about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. By 2039 I'm fifty-six, the house is paid off, and we could rent the land out to someone with robots and live on that. I'd miss the cattle, but I wouldn't be poor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am for most of the ten years. Kenji and I would make a plan to step back around 2038, renting out the land and keeping a few cattle as a hobby. I'd tell Ellie and Sam they don't have to farm, but the land's there if they want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. More settled than in any of the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ellie and Sam about the farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the land isn't going anywhere, even if the jobs on it change. I'd tell my kids that land is the one thing a robot can't make more of, so we're keeping Lower Fold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you uneasy even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenji. If he wanted to sell up and I didn't, that's a fight I'd hate. But we've agreed on most things for twenty years, so I'd hope we'd agree on that too.

say: I'd say ten years is **ten harvests**, plenty of time to sort it.
I'd **not get worked up** about it in public.
think: It **suits me**: by 2039 I'm fifty-six with the house paid off.
We could **rent the land** to someone with robots and live on that.
do: Keep farming **as I am** for most of the ten years.
Plan with Kenji to **step back around 2038** and rent out the land.
Tell Ellie and Sam the **land stays** if they want it.
feel: **Calm**, more settled than in any other picture.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids that land is the one thing a robot can't make more of, so we're keeping Lower Fold.
fieldNote: Landownership turns robots into a **rental income**, not a threat.
His only worry is a possible **disagreement with Kenji**.
He sees land as the **family's anchor** whatever the jobs become.

steps.text: Keep farming cattle and potatoes as now until the late 2030s
Step back around 2038 and rent the land to a robot farmer
Tell Ellie and Sam the land stays in the family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because we'd have to decide too fast and I'm not built for fast. What would help is the government keeping prices fair, so the big robot farms can't push family farms out. Some honest advice on which machines actually work would help too, not from someone selling them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what farming is for. I don't farm because it pays best, I farm because my dad's name is still on the gate at Lower Fold.

headlineQuote: I don't farm because it pays best, I farm because my dad's name is still on the gate at Lower Fold.
portrait: Yusuf co-owns **Lower Fold Farm** with his brother Kenji and does the hands-on cattle and potatoes.
He has **never used AI**, leaves paperwork to Kenji, and waits years before copying neighbours.
Owning **land and savings** keeps him calm in most pictures, though fast AGI makes him anxious.
His fear is being **the slow one** while robot-run farms set the prices.
Given time, he'd **rent the land out** and step back around fifty-six.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to make decisions faster than he's built for.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair prices** so big robot farms can't push family farms out.
**Honest advice** on which machines work, from someone not selling them.
